title: The conquerors
hook: emperors who conquered every land, with drums beating, also went without the Name (Savaiye)

segments.voice: Yesterday, maate matang, maddened elephants, and your line, they left empty-handed. Today, a verse you can hear before you see it.

Before you see an army in the old world, you hear it. A low thudding comes over the hills, then another and another, until the ground itself seems to beat. Kettledrums, war drums, the big nagaras, carried in front of the march so every village knows who's coming. Kings had them beaten when they set out and again when they came home with a new country in their pocket. Now listen for the moment after the march has passed, when the last beat rolls away down the valley.
screen: `A THUDDING OVER THE HILLS.` → `NAGARAS IN FRONT OF THE MARCH.` → `THE LAST BEAT ROLLS AWAY.`

segments.voice: Among the ten savaiye is a verse made of that sound. In paraphrase: they went out and conquered every land in every direction, with drums and kettledrums beating. Their elephants trumpeted, their horses neighed by the thousand. Kings like these, past, present and to come, can't be counted. Then the turn the savaiye keep making: without remembering the Lord, at the end they all went to their final home. Beside it stands another savaiya, about warriors in shining armor so sure of themselves they thought even mountains couldn't move them. They too go. The striking thing is the man writing it. Guru Gobind Singh had a great drum of his own. Sikh tradition remembers the Ranjit Nagara, a huge kettledrum made at Anandpur, beaten morning and evening, whose boom worried the hill kings around him. Sikhs still beat a nagara at some gurdwaras and in processions today. So this isn't someone who hated drums; he knew how good it felt to hear your own. The verse's point is simpler and harder. The sound of victory is real, and it fades. The conquerors are measured not by how far their drums carried, but by whether they remembered the One who outlasts every march. In the Sikh view, that remembering, simran, is what keeps sounding after the last beat. So the verse is said in the quiet of early morning, before the day's own drums start up: deadlines, targets, scoreboards. They're allowed to beat. The verse just counts how long each one lasts.
screen: `THEY CONQUERED EVERY LAND.` · `WITHOUT THE NAME, THEY STILL WENT.` · `THE GURU'S OWN GREAT DRUM.` · `VICTORY IS REAL, AND IT FADES.` · then, large: `DRUMS FADE.`

segments.voice: Listen for a minute to the sounds around you, near and far, and notice how each one rises and fades. Then find one small thing you've been pushing for mostly to be seen winning, more likes, the last word, being first, and hold it lightly, like a drumbeat already rolling away. You don't have to give up every goal; if you pray, say Waheguru as you set this one down.
The conquerors. A savaiya of kettledrums and conquered lands: kings beyond counting, who at the end still went without the Name.
Your line: drums fade. Remembering keeps sounding. Three hundred sixty-five days: a whole year of days, walked.

screen: `DAY 365 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: EYES SHUT LIKE A CRANE.`

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this among the Tav Prasad Savaiye each morning, and the nagara, the great kettledrum, is still beaten at some gurdwaras and in Sikh processions.

fork.setup: you're a king. your drums have carried your name across every land and your horses number in the thousands. what does the savaiya say comes next?
options: without the Name, at the end you go, like the rest.
fork.reveal: the verse lets the drums beat and the elephants trumpet, then follows the kings to their final home. without remembering the Lord, the march ends where every march ends.

original.note: Gurmukhi: nagaare, kettledrums, among the drums beating in this savaiya's conquering march.

trapdoor: what you thought: a verse against war.
what it means: the drums of victory are real and they fade; the conquerors are measured by whether they remembered the Lord.
what a scholar hears: the writer kept a great drum of his own, the Ranjit Nagara, so the verse speaks from inside the world of courts and campaigns, not from outside it.

chat.says: If a king conquered every land, isn't that a life that really counted?
options: Victory is real, but it fades; without remembering the Lord, at the end they still went.
Yes; the savaiya says kings who win every land are remembered forever.

chat.meaning: The drum savaiya lets the drums beat, then says: without remembering the Lord, at the end they all went to their final home.

nagaras.meaning: big kettledrums carried before a march

Ranjit Nagara.meaning: the great drum tradition remembers at Anandpur

simran.meaning: remembering the One, often by repeating the Name

Anandpur.meaning: the Tenth Guru's town in the hills of Punjab

recall: the ego that says I did this alone

notes: The drum savaiya (jeet phire sabh des disaan ko baajat dhol mridang nagaare ...) paraphrased; usually counted as one of savaiyas 3–7. The voice says 'among the ten' without a number. Confirm its place and the paraphrase of its last line.
The armored-warriors savaiya (sudh sipaah durant dubaah ...) mentioned briefly as standing beside it. Confirm.
Ranjit Nagara: tradition dates it to the 1680s at Anandpur and says its sound alarmed the hill rajas (Bhim Chand of Bilaspur). Given as 'Sikh tradition remembers'. Confirm.
Nagara still beaten at some gurdwaras and in processions (nagar kirtan): confirm.
